description: Team CCTI: Romeo Decu (team owner) and Cristina Simion, from Romania. We work on thermodynamics and informatics; combustion science was new to us, so we built GFL to be checked rather than trusted: every result is measured from NASA's public data, signed in a ledger, and re-verifiable by anyone. We built it with AI assistance, documented in full.
summary: Gravity Fire Ledger (GFL) is a microgravity combustion analysis platform that turns NASA's public combustion data into evidence a fire-safety engineer can check. NASA's own BASS results show that the standard ground flammability test is not conservative in microgravity, so evidence does not carry over by default. GFL answers three questions that are usually mixed up: does a source address my question, were the conditions comparable, and can a finding be carried to another context? GFL measured flame-spread rates from NASA's raw BASS-II images under rules frozen before they were run, sealed every step in a signed ledger your browser re-verifies, and mapped all 24 combustion investigations in NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics repository by fire-safety function, from ignition to suppression. Three AI models from three providers extract what NASA's records state, every value is checked word for word against the record, and fixed rules decide what may transfer. The honest result: at record level, no pair of investigations can be said to transfer; GFL shows, pair by pair, what is missing. Applied to Apollo 1: none of the NASA records GFL read report flame spread over solid materials in enriched oxygen. Knowing where the evidence stops makes fire-safety decisions defensible.
details:
What it does

GFL is a web platform for anyone who must decide what NASA's microgravity fire experiments do and do not tell them: a spacecraft fire-safety engineer, a researcher planning the next experiment, a reviewer. It keeps three questions apart. Relevance: does an experiment address my question? Comparability: were its conditions the ones I care about, and are they recorded? Transferability: may a finding inform another context, within what stated limits? Unknown is never treated as compatible, a conflict between sources is not treated as a physical difference, and a value reported by a source is never presented as a GFL measurement.

How it works

1. Measurement from NASA's raw data. From the raw camera stills of the BASS-II investigation (PSI-25), GFL measures the luminous-edge spread rate of a thin PMMA film in microgravity. The rule that picks the frames and the edge was frozen and anchored in the ledger before it was run; B6 had been seen under earlier rules, and the record says so. Result for run B6: 2.20 mm/s (95 % interval 1.91–2.37). Five more runs were measured with the same rule (B9, B11, B13, B19, B20); B16 was attempted and is not measurable under it. The two at 17 % oxygen burn at about half the rate of B6, an exploratory comparison: the flows differ and it was not pre-registered. Four predictions were sealed before their runs were downloaded: one supported, one not supported, two not testable; all four are shown.

2. A signed ledger. Every input file, rule, result and decision is a hash-chained entry signed with Ed25519 and anchored to Git commits and external time stamps. The page re-verifies all entries in the visitor's browser. One command rebuilds the results in an empty copy and compares them with the sealed fingerprints: 34 of 34 identical from NASA's raw files.

3. A fire-safety evidence map. For the 24 investigations NASA lists under Combustion Science, three AI models from three providers (grok-4.7, Kimi-K2.6, gpt-5.5) read NASA's record text and fill one form: fuel phase, gravity, flow, atmosphere, and the fire-safety functions served. A value is kept only if its quoted passage is found word for word in NASA's record, and only if all three models give it. NASA and IBM’s INDUS language model measures relevance, separately, and flags quotes for a human reading. Fixed rules then decide, for all 276 pairs of investigations, whether a finding may be carried: 97 share no fire-safety function, 98 are not directly transferable because a recorded condition differs, 81 are not established because a condition is not stated, and none is conditionally informative on record text alone. A matrix shows every pair; one click gives the reason.

4. One level down. 20 of the 24 investigations also publish a table with one row per run. GFL inventories what those tables record and shows that evidence beside each open condition. It also works one transfer end to end from them: Saffire-II's 5 cm fabric strips spread at 2.1–2.6 mm/s according to NASA; the Saffire-I sample, eight times wider, gives 2.24 mm/s from its length and burn time. Conditionally informative as a comparison of reported values; undetermined as a quantitative transfer, because no uncertainty is reported. GFL then tried to measure Saffire from the images under two rules frozen in advance; both failed, and both failures are reported, not tuned away.

5. Real incidents. For Apollo 1, Apollo 13 and the Mir fire, GFL lists the functions involved and what the archive holds for them. Apollo 1 burned in pure oxygen: no investigation's record text states an enriched atmosphere, and the two run tables that record oxygen above 30 % (PSI-10, PSI-159) are not solid-fuel investigations. That is what these records hold, not proof that no such experiment exists.

Benefits and intended impact

GFL makes NASA's combustion archive usable for decisions that must be defended: it shows what was measured, how sure we are, what carries over and why the rest does not. The method is not tied to fire: the ledger, frozen rules and quote-checked extraction can be applied to any experimental archive. Three directions are specified but not built: enriched-oxygen cabins for exploration vehicles, partial gravity for the Moon and Mars, and confined low-flow fires on Earth.

What the data cannot settle, and the next question

NASA's images show the luminous edge of the flame, not the pyrolysis front; the flow speed at the sample surface was not recorded; each condition was flown once. GFL states these limits beside its results. The next research question is how far independent evidence, such as a second observable, a flow model or a matched ground test, can bound what a single flight image cannot. Saffire's backlit cameras, which record the burn front in transmission, are one such second observable.

How it was built

Two people, Romeo Decu and Cristina Simion, set the questions, made every decision and approved each step. AI models in declared roles wrote the code and analyses and attacked the results; GFL re-ran their work rather than trusting it. Coordination ran through AAL, the team's own orchestration software.

Tools

Python 3.10+ (NumPy, SciPy, rawpy, Pillow, cryptography), JavaScript with Plotly.js, Cytoscape.js and ELK.js, HTML and CSS, Git and GitHub Actions (tests on Python 3.10 to 3.13, ledger verification and browser tests in Chromium and Firefox on every change), Azure AI Foundry for the extraction models, sentence-transformers for INDUS, Playwright for browser tests. It runs on any computer with Python: double-click START_GFL.bat (Windows) or run START_GFL.sh.

Creativity

Most tools ask "which data look relevant?". GFL asks what a finding is allowed to say about another experiment, and shows its own failures: a prediction that did not hold, two measurement rules that failed, a pair that stopped being transferable when a third model was added. Every claim can be checked by re-execution in the visitor's own browser.
